title: Khaybar and Safiyyah
hook: after Khaybar, Safiyyah, daughter of a Jewish chief, becomes his wife and a mother of the believers

segments.voice: Yesterday, Heraclius, and letters honest and short. Your line was sealed and sent.

Some people's lives turn completely in a single week. Safiyyah's did. She was the daughter of Huyayy, a chief of the Jewish tribe of Banu an-Nadir, a young woman from one of the most respected families of the old Jewish communities of Arabia. Her people had once lived in Medina, been expelled after conflict with the Muslims, and settled in Khaybar, a rich oasis of date palms and stone forts north of the city. Some of their leaders had helped rally the great army at the Trench. In the seventh year after the migration, the Muslims marched on Khaybar. When it was over, her husband was dead, and she was a captive.
screen: `A CHIEF'S DAUGHTER.` → `AN OASIS OF FORTS.` → `ONE WEEK, EVERYTHING CHANGES.`

segments.voice: The Muslim sources tell what happened next briefly. Sahih al-Bukhari says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ freed Safiyyah and married her, and made her freedom her dowry. An early biographer, Ibn Sa'd, adds that he gave her a choice: to go free, back to her people, or to become Muslim and marry him, and that she chose him. The sources say much less about what she felt that week, and it's honest to say so. Modern readers, Muslim and not, have asked hard questions about a marriage made in the aftermath of a battle, and Muslim scholars have answered with what the sources report of her choice and of the marriage that followed. What the sources do keep are small, clear moments. Bukhari says that when they set out, the Prophet sat by his camel and put out his knee, and Safiyyah stepped on his knee to mount. And at-Tirmidhi keeps a hadith from later on. Some of the other wives teased her, calling her the daughter of a Jew, and she came to the Prophet in tears. He told her: say to them, my father is Aaron, my uncle is Moses, and my husband is Muhammad. What do you have over me? He didn't ask her to hide where she came from. He told her it was a lineage of prophets, Muslims' prophets too. Safiyyah lived for decades after him, known for her generosity and good sense. The Qur'an calls the Prophet's wives mothers of the believers, and she is one of them: a woman from Khaybar, honored by her full name, and by her family.
screen: `FREED, AND HER FREEDOM HER DOWRY.` · `THE SOURCES SAY LITTLE OF HER HEART.` · `SHE STEPPED ON HIS KNEE.` · `MY FATHER IS AARON.` · then, large: `A MOTHER OF BELIEVERS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose family, faith, country or language is different from yours, maybe someone who's been teased for it, and of what their background has given them, and given you through them. Picture one way you could honor it: asking about it, remembering a holiday, saying their name the way they say it.
Safiyyah, the chief's daughter from Khaybar who became the Prophet's wife and a mother of the believers.
Your line: a mother of believers. A lineage of prophets, nothing to hide. Day two hundred seventy-six, done.

howItsDone: Muslims honor the Prophet's wives as mothers of the believers, following 33:6, and Safiyyah bint Huyayy is often remembered through the hadith of 'my father is Aaron, my uncle is Moses'.
